sowhat.text: A 2% AI-led drop, a 10-year at 5.04% and Waller pointing to a 50 bp hike make for a tougher tape, though high yield spreads at 347 bp show credit is still open. Strategic stock deals and energy buyouts are still getting done, and the record Anthropic raise shows equity demand for AI is deep.

pitch: Stocks sold off hard on Thursday. The S&P 500 fell 2 percent to about 7,176, its sixth straight loss, the Dow dropped 2.2 percent and the Nasdaq 2.3 percent, as worries grew that the AI boom is overheating. The VIX jumped to about 28. Rates are the backdrop: the Fed minutes showed almost everyone expects more hikes, Governor Waller wants a half-point in December, and the 10-year closed at 5.04 percent. Oil was steady, with WTI near 83 dollars and Brent near 92. On deals, Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy Applied Compute for 4.5 billion dollars in stock, and ECP closed its EnergySolutions buyout. Anthropic raised a record 81 billion dollars in its IPO and closed up 17 percent.

quiz.q: Where did the S&P 500 close on Thursday 19 Nov?
quiz.a: 7,176, down 2.0% and the sixth straight loss.

quiz.q: Why did stocks fall on 19 Nov even though Anthropic's debut went well?
quiz.a: Worries that the AI boom is overheating, with chipmakers leading and AMD hit by a short-seller report, plus expectations of higher US rates.

quiz.q: How is Palo Alto Networks paying for Applied Compute, and for how much?
quiz.a: All stock, valued at $4.5B, expected to close in its fiscal Q3 2027.

chat.a: Stocks sold off on Thursday: the S&P 500 fell 2.0% to 7,176, the Dow 2.2% and the Nasdaq 2.3%, on worries the AI boom is overheating. The Fed minutes pointed to more hikes and the 10-year closed at 5.04%. Anthropic's record IPO went well but did not stop the slide.
chat.tip: Lead with the AI selloff, then rates.

chat.q: What's your read on oil this week?
chat.a: WTI settled at $83.21 and Brent at $91.98, both flat on Thursday after a drop on Wednesday, a spread of about $9. Oil is steady for now, but lower prices pressure upstream valuations and make energy buyers and sellers harder to match on price.
chat.tip: Say what would change your view.

chat.a: Palo Alto Networks agreed to buy Applied Compute for $4.5B in stock on 18 Nov. ECP closed its EnergySolutions buyout on 16 Nov, with Morgan Stanley and RBC advising EnergySolutions.
chat.tip: Name the advisers; bankers will ask.

chat.q: What are you watching over the next few weeks?
chat.a: The December 8-9 FOMC, where Waller has argued for a half-point hike, and whether the AI selloff continues after Anthropic's debut. Both drive financing conditions, since the 10-year is 5.04% and the S&P 500 is down six sessions in a row.
chat.tip: Tie each event to financing conditions.

chat.q: If the 10-year rose 50 bp, what happens to a DCF?
chat.a: The 10-year is 5.04% now. A 50 bp rise lifts the risk-free rate and so the WACC, which lowers the present value of cash flows. Long-duration assets with most of their value in the terminal value are hit hardest.
chat.tip: Say the direction, then who is hit hardest.

chat.q: How do high rates affect a sponsor deal like ECP and EnergySolutions?
chat.a: A 10-year at 5.04% and a Fed possibly hiking 50 bp raise the cost of acquisition debt, which squeezes sponsor returns unless the price adjusts. High yield spreads were 347 bp on 18 Nov, so credit is available, just at a high all-in cost.
chat.tip: Separate the base rate from the credit spread.

chat.q: Why would an acquirer pay in stock, as Palo Alto Networks is doing for Applied Compute?
chat.a: An all-stock deal avoids borrowing at today's high rates, with the 10-year at 5.04%, and shares risk with the target's owners. The catch is dilution and exposure to the acquirer's share price, which matters more after a 2% down day for the S&P 500.
